sections.title: What a graphic designer invoice must show
sections.body: A standard invoice leaves too much room for client assumptions. As a graphic designer, your invoice must explicitly define the boundaries of your project. You are not just billing for hours spent at a screen. You are billing for specific outputs, intellectual property, and agreed timelines. If you bundle everything into a single line item, clients will assume source files and unlimited tweaks are included. Break down your services clearly. Use our free invoice generator at /tools/free-invoice-generator to create an itemised document that separates your creative labour from final asset delivery and copyright transfers.
items: Separate line items for design concepts and final assets
Explicit licensing terms and commercial usage rights
Cost of native source file handover if requested

sections.title: How graphic designer work is usually priced and billed
sections.body: Graphic design is rarely billed by the hour because experienced designers work faster than beginners. Most professionals use value-based pricing or flat project fees. This means your invoice should reflect the project scope rather than time spent. When billing a flat fee, you must define revision rounds. A single round typically includes minor text or colour tweaks, while a completely new concept requires a new line item. If a client needs a logo by tomorrow, add a rush fee line item to compensate for the disrupted schedule and prioritised focus.
items: Flat project fees based on the final agreed deliverables
Specific line items for additional revision rounds
Rush fees applied as a percentage of the total

sections.title: Getting paid: terms, deposits and chasing late clients
sections.body: Never start a design project without a deposit. A standard practice is billing fifty percent upfront to secure your time and commit the client to the process. Send this initial invoice before you sketch a single concept. Once the work is approved, send the final invoice with a clear payment deadline. Do not release high-resolution files or transfer copyright until the final balance clears your bank account. If a client delays payment, send polite but firm reminders referencing the agreed terms and withholding the final deliverables until the account is settled.

faqs.q: Should I charge extra for the native source files?
faqs.a: Yes. When a client pays for a design, they are usually paying for the final exported asset, like a flattened PDF or PNG. The native source files contain your proprietary layer structures and methods. If a client wants these files so another designer can edit them later, you should bill this as a separate line item. This compensates you for the loss of future update work.

faqs.q: How do I bill for extra revision rounds?
faqs.a: Your initial quote and invoice should state exactly how many revision rounds are included in the flat fee. If a client requests changes beyond that limit, you must issue a new line item or a separate invoice for the extra work. Clearly define what constitutes a revision. Changing a font colour is a minor tweak, but requesting a completely new layout is a new concept that requires additional billing.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a design fee and a licensing fee?
faqs.a: The design fee covers the labour and expertise required to create the visual concept. The licensing fee covers the client's right to use that artwork commercially. Many designers separate these on their invoices. A small local business might pay a lower licensing fee for a logo than a national corporation, even if the design labour took the exact same amount of time.

faqs.q: How much should I charge for a rush fee?
faqs.a: Rush fees typically range from twenty-five to one hundred percent of the standard project fee, depending on the urgency and how much it disrupts your schedule. Add this as a distinct line item on your invoice. This makes it clear to the client that they are paying a premium for speed, and it prevents them from expecting that same rapid turnaround for standard pricing in the future.
